english: I'm here to look at a place
usage: I came to look at a place
Polite; what you say walking into a 부동산 (real estate office)
I'm here to see a place
반말, only with a friend tagging along, not to the agent
I've come to look at places
Formal 합쇼체, a touch stiffer/more businesslike
I came to look at a room
Swap 방 ('room') when you want a one-room/studio (원룸)
examples: 안녕하세요, 집 보러 왔는데요.
Hi, I'm here to look at a place.
The standard opener the moment you step into the office; the -는데요 signals you're ready for the agent to take over
A: 원룸 보러 왔는데요, 지금 볼 수 있는 거 있어요? / B: 네, 몇 가지 준비해 뒀어요. 예산이 어떻게 되세요?
A: I came to see studios — anything I can view now? / B: Yes, I've got a few ready. What's your budget?
원룸 specifies the type; 볼 수 있는 거 asks what's viewable today; the agent's reply shows how -는데요 hands the conversation over naturally
학교 근처에 집 보러 왔는데요, 예산은 한 오백에 오십이요.
I'm here to look at places near the school; my budget's roughly 5 million deposit and 500k a month.
한 ('about') + 오백/오십 states 보증금/월세 in 만원 units — say this right after the opener so the agent filters listings for you
nuance: 집 보러 왔는데요 is 집 ('house/home') + 보러 (the -러 'in order to' form of 보다 'to see') + 왔- (past of 오다 'come') + -는데요, a soft sentence-ender that introduces a topic and invites the listener to respond. Literally 'I came in order to see places, and…' — the universal first line when you walk into a 부동산 (real-estate office). Here 보다 does NOT mean 'watch'; in the housing context it specifically means 'view/inspect a property', the way English says 'look at a place'. The nearest near-synonym is 집 구하러 왔는데요 ('I came to find/secure a place'), but the stage differs: 보러 signals you're ready to physically walk through rooms today, while 구하러 frames the broader search for housing. The English-speaker trap is dropping -는데요 for a flat 집 보러 왔어요, which is correct but blunter and doesn't invite the agent to take over. A worse trap is saying 집 찾으러 왔어요 — 찾다 ('to search for something lost') is wrong register for an agent-office visit; Koreans say 보러 or 구하러 here, never 찾으러. Keep 존댓말 with any agent; 반말 to a stranger doing business is jarringly rude.

structuredNuance.t: 집 + 보러 (to see, purpose form of 보다) + 왔- (came) + -는데요 (soft topic-opener). Literally 'I came in order to see places, and…'. Here 보다 does NOT mean 'watch'; it means 'view/inspect a property'. The -는데요 ending invites the agent to respond ('what's your budget? this way…') — it is not just filler.

This is the very first line when you walk through the door of any 부동산 (real-estate office). Always 존댓말 with an agent who is a professional stranger. The full formal variant 집 좀 보러 왔습니다 (합쇼체) is fine but sounds stiffer. 반말 (집 보러 왔어) is only appropriate when speaking to a friend who came with you, never to the agent.

집 구하러 왔는데요 ('I came to find/secure a place') differs in stage: 보러 means you're here to view units today; 구하러 frames the whole house-hunting mission. Both are natural, but 보러 is the standard opener when you're ready to physically walk through rooms.
Swap 집 for 방 (방 보러 왔는데요) when looking for a studio/one-room. Add your type upfront: 원룸 보러 왔는데요, 오피스텔 보러 왔는데요. For formal contexts use 집 좀 보러 왔습니다.

Two traps: (1) Saying 집 찾으러 왔어요 — 찾다 is for searching for a lost object; at a real-estate office Koreans say 보러 or 구하러, never 찾으러. (2) Dropping -는데요 to get 집 보러 왔어요 — grammatically correct but blunt; the soft -는데요 is what makes the opener sound like a real customer easing in.

mistakes: Saying 집 봐 주세요 to mean 'show me a place'.
봐 주세요 means 'please look at it (for me)' — as if asking the agent to inspect something on your behalf. To say you've come to view places, say 집 보러 왔는데요; to be shown one, 집 좀 보여 주세요.
Dropping -는데요 and stating a flat 집 보러 왔어요.
It's correct but abrupt as an opener. The soft ender 집 보러 왔는데요 hands the conversation to the agent and sounds like a real customer easing in.
Using 찾으러 instead of 보러/구하러.
찾다 is 'to search for' a lost or hidden thing. For house-hunting at an office, Koreans say 보러 왔어요 (to view) or 집 구하러 왔어요 (to secure a place), not 찾으러 왔어요.

english: Is it monthly rent or jeonse?
usage: Is it monthly rent or jeonse?
Polite; asking which rental scheme a listing is
반말, comparing options with a friend
Would this be monthly or jeonse?
반전세 = big deposit + smaller monthly, the in-between type
examples: 이 집 월세예요, 전세예요?
Is this place monthly rent or jeonse?
Pointing at one listing to pin down the scheme — ask this before any other money question
A: 전세는 부담돼서요, 월세로 보고 있어요. / B: 그러시면 보증금 천에 월 오십 정도 보여 드릴게요.
A: Jeonse is too much for me, so I'm looking at monthly. / B: In that case I'll show you places around 10M deposit and 500k a month.
부담되다 ('to be a burden') explains your preference; the agent's response shows how amounts are stated in 만원 units
보증금 천에 월 오십이면 반전세네요?
10 million deposit and 500k a month — that's semi-jeonse, right?
Naming the deposit/monthly split to confirm it's 반전세 — use this to show you understand the system
nuance: 월세 (月貰) and 전세 (傳貰) are the two pillars of Korean renting, so you'll ask this constantly. 월세 means you pay a deposit (보증금) plus rent every month, like renting in most countries. 전세 is uniquely Korean: you hand the landlord one enormous lump sum — often 50–80% of the home's market value — for the whole lease term, pay zero monthly rent, and get every won back at move-out; the landlord profits by investing your money. A third type, 반전세 ('half-jeonse'), sits in the middle: a larger-than-월세 deposit plus a smaller monthly fee. The key distinction learners blur is 보증금 vs. 전세금: in 월세 the deposit is a modest security 보증금; in 전세 that lump sum IS the rent mechanism (전세금/전셋돈) and is not a 'deposit' in the Western sense. The copula trap: after a vowel-ending noun, Korean contracts 이에요 to 예요, so it must be 월세예요, 전세예요 — saying 월세이에요 is the uncontracted, unnatural form. Always 존댓말 with an agent.

structuredNuance.t: 월세 (月貰, 'monthly rent') and 전세 (傳貰, 'jeonse') name the two dominant Korean rental schemes. The question is literally 'Is it monthly-rent, or is it jeonse?' — but it carries the full weight of asking which financial structure you're dealing with, since the two involve completely different sums and obligations.

Ask this the moment a listing catches your interest, before discussing price. 존댓말 is always required with an agent. The softer 월세인가요, 전세인가요? (with -인가요) is natural when asking tentatively about a listing you're not sure about yet.

The confusion is 보증금 vs. 전세금: in 월세, 보증금 is a modest returnable security deposit; in 전세, 전세금 is the entire rent-replacing lump sum — it is not a 'deposit' in the Western sense because there is no additional monthly rent at all. 반전세 ('half-jeonse') = large deposit + reduced monthly, the middle ground.
반전세예요? confirms the in-between type. You can also ask 어떤 방식이에요? ('what's the arrangement?') for a more open question. For clarity on semi-jeonse ask 보증금이랑 월세가 얼마씩이에요? ('how much each?').

Two traps: (1) Calling 전세금 a 'deposit' and expecting to also pay monthly — with true 전세 there is no monthly payment at all; the lump sum IS the rent. (2) Saying 월세이에요 — after a vowel-ending noun the copula contracts: 월세예요, 전세예요. 월세이에요 is the uncontracted, unnatural form.

mistakes: Thinking 전세 means 'deposit' on top of monthly rent.
With 전세 you pay a huge lump sum and NO monthly rent, getting it all back at move-out. If there's monthly rent plus a deposit, that's 월세 (or 반전세), not 전세.
Confusing 보증금 with 전세금.
보증금 is the (usually smaller) security deposit in a 월세 contract; 전세금 is the whole lease sum in 전세. They aren't the same number or the same idea — ask 보증금 얼마예요? for 월세, 전세금 얼마예요? for 전세.
Saying 월세이에요 instead of 월세예요.
After the vowel-ending 월세, the copula contracts to 예요: 월세예요, 전세예요. 월세이에요 is the uncontracted, unnatural form.

usage: Polite; the first money question on any 월세 listing
반말, with a friend comparing places
Softer, 'how does the deposit work out?' — very natural to agents
Negotiating: trade a lower 보증금 for higher 월세
examples: 여기 보증금 얼마예요?
How much is the deposit here?
Asked while looking at a specific unit; no particle needed before 얼마예요?
A: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요? / B: 천에 오십이요.
A: What's the deposit situation? / B: 10 million deposit, 500k a month.
어떻게 돼요? is the softer, more natural agent-question form; 천/오십 in 만원 units is the everyday way to state amounts
보증금을 조금 올리면 월세 좀 깎아 주실 수 있어요?
If I raise the deposit a bit, could you lower the monthly rent?
The classic 보증금↑ → 월세↓ trade, asked politely with 깎다 — show you understand how the system works
nuance: 보증금 (保證金, 'security/guarantee deposit') is the up-front lump sum the landlord holds against unpaid rent or damage, returned in full when you leave. In Korean renting, 보증금 and 월세 slide against each other: a higher deposit buys a lower monthly rent and vice versa, so asking 보증금 얼마예요? is really asking where this unit sits on that scale. Amounts are spoken in 만원 (10,000-won) units — '천' means 천만 원 (10 million) and '오십' means 오십만 원 (500k); you almost never say the full digits. The agent-friendly variant 보증금이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does the deposit come out?') is softer and more conversational than the bare 얼마예요?. The dividing line from 전세금 is which contract you're in: 보증금 is part of a 월세 arrangement; 전세금 replaces monthly rent entirely — never ask 전세금 얼마예요? about a 월세 listing. Particle tip: with 얼마예요? you can drop the subject particle (보증금 얼마예요?), but with 어떻게 돼요? add 이: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요?. The English-speaker trap is treating 보증금 like 'first-and-last month's rent' — it is a single negotiable lump, often 10–20× the monthly rent, not a standard two-month figure. Stay in 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: 보증금 (保證金) literally means 'guarantee money' — the lump sum that guarantees the tenant's obligations. In practice it anchors the entire financial structure of the 월세 rental: the higher it is, the lower the monthly rent tends to be. Asking 보증금 얼마예요? is really asking 'where does this unit sit on the deposit-rent sliding scale?'

Ask after confirming the rental type is 월세. 존댓말 always. The variant 보증금이 어떻게 돼요? is softer and preferred in conversation with an agent; 보증금 얼마예요? is equally correct but slightly more direct. 반말 (보증금 얼마야?) only with a friend, never the agent.

보증금 (월세 security deposit) vs. 전세금 (전세 lump sum): they sound similar but belong to different contract types. Don't ask 전세금 얼마예요? about a 월세 listing. The trade-off expression: 보증금을 올리면 월세를 낮출 수 있어요 — raise one to lower the other.
보증금이 어떻게 돼요? (softer). 보증금 좀 낮출 수 있어요? (negotiate down). 보증금을 올리면 월세 깎아 주세요 (offer to raise it for a rent cut). In listings the shorthand is 보증금/월세: 500/50 means 5M deposit / 500k monthly.

Two traps: (1) Treating 보증금 as 'first-and-last month's rent' — it is a single negotiable lump, often far larger (10–20× the monthly). (2) Particle mix-up: 보증금 얼마예요? (no particle fine); but 보증금'이' 어떻게 돼요? needs 이. Mixing these up sounds off.

mistakes: Reading '천' as 1,000 won instead of 천만 원.
Housing amounts are in 만원 units. 천 means 천만 원 (10 million); 오십 means 오십만 원 (500k). Hearing '보증금 천' as a literal 1,000 won will mis-set your whole budget.
Saying 보증금이 얼마예요 vs 보증금이 어떻게 돼요 with the wrong particle.
With 얼마예요? Koreans usually drop the particle (보증금 얼마예요?). With 어떻게 돼요? keep 이: 보증금이 어떻게 돼요?. Mixing them sounds off.
Treating 보증금 like Western first-and-last-month rent.
보증금 is one lump tied to the rent scheme, often many times the monthly rent, and it slides against 월세. It is not 'two months' rent up front'; ask the actual figure and the trade-off.

usage: Polite; checking what's on top of rent
The flip side: asking if it's already baked in
What does the maintenance fee cover?
Drilling into what the 관리비 includes (water? internet?)
examples: 월세 말고 관리비는 따로예요?
Apart from rent, is there a separate maintenance fee?
월세 말고 ('aside from rent') frames it as a potential hidden cost — always ask this
A: 관리비 얼마예요? 거기에 수도세 포함이에요? / B: 오만 원이고, 수도세는 별도예요.
A: How much is the maintenance fee? Does it include water? / B: 50,000 won, and water is separate.
Always follow up with what's included; 별도 ('separate/extra') is the key word in the agent's answer
관리비에 인터넷이랑 청소 포함이면 괜찮네요.
If internet and cleaning are in the maintenance fee, that's not bad.
Weigh the 관리비 by what's bundled — internet + cleaning included can make a higher 관리비 worthwhile
nuance: 관리비 (管理費, 'management/maintenance fee') is the monthly building charge billed ON TOP of your rent, covering cleaning of common areas, the elevator, security, hallway lighting, and possibly water (수도세), internet, or heating depending on the building. In a small 원룸 it might be 30,000–50,000 won; in a large apartment complex it can be much more. The question 관리비는 따로예요? ('is it separate?') is essential because a cheap-looking 월세 can hide a fat 관리비. Always follow up with 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? because what it bundles varies wildly. The dividing line is 따로 ('separate/on top') vs. 포함 (包含, 'included'): 관리비는 따로예요? assumes it might be extra and asks if so; 관리비 포함이에요? assumes it might be built in and asks if so — they expect opposite yes/no answers, so pick the one you mean. The English-speaker trap is assuming 관리비 is like a Western HOA fee paid only by owners — Korean renters pay it every month too. Another trap is skipping the follow-up: a '관리비 포함' listing might only include lighting, not water or internet, so the bundled items matter. The topic particle 는 on 관리비는 따로예요? sets up a contrast ('as for the maintenance fee…') and is the natural form; dropping it casually is fine. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent.

structuredNuance.t: 관리비 (管理費) literally means 'management fee'. 따로예요? asks 'is it separate/apart?' — together the question means 'Is the maintenance fee billed on top of the rent, or is it included?' The real point is to catch hidden costs: a low 월세 listing is often paired with a high 관리비.

Ask this immediately after learning the 월세 amount. 존댓말 with the agent always. The flip phrasing 관리비 포함이에요? (asking 'is it included?') is equally natural — pick whichever matches your assumption. 반말 (관리비 따로야?) only with a friend.

따로 ('separate/apart') vs. 포함 ('included'): these are the two poles of the answer. 관리비는 따로예요? and 관리비 포함이에요? ask the same thing from opposite angles — they cannot both be answered 'yes' simultaneously, so be clear which you're asking.
관리비 포함이에요? (included?). 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? (what's in it?). 관리비 말고 따로 내는 게 있어요? ('anything else to pay beyond 관리비?'). Always ask the follow-up to know what's actually covered.

Two traps: (1) Assuming 관리비 is like a Western owner-only HOA fee — Korean renters pay it monthly too, so budget 월세 + 관리비 + utilities. (2) Conflating 따로 and 포함 — they expect opposite answers, so using the wrong one gives you the wrong information.

mistakes: Ignoring 관리비 because the rent looks cheap.
A low 월세 can hide a high 관리비. Always ask 관리비 얼마예요? and 관리비에 뭐가 포함돼요? — the real monthly cost is 월세 + 관리비.
Mixing up 따로 and 포함.
관리비는 따로예요? asks if it's a separate extra charge; 관리비 포함이에요? asks if it's already included in rent. They expect opposite answers — pick the one you mean.
Assuming renters don't pay 관리비.
Unlike a Western owners-only HOA fee, Korean renters pay 관리비 every month on top of rent. Budget for 월세 + 관리비 + utilities, not rent alone.

usage: Polite; asking what comes with the place
풀옵션 = fridge, washer, AC, bed, etc. all included
Asking about one specific 옵션 item
examples: 여기 옵션은 뭐가 있어요?
What's included here?
General check of what appliances/furniture come with the unit — ask this during every viewing
A: 풀옵션이에요? 세탁기랑 냉장고 다 있어요? / B: 네, 에어컨이랑 인덕션도 있어요.
A: Is it full-option? Are the washer and fridge both there? / B: Yes, and there's AC and an induction stove too.
Confirm 풀옵션 then check specific items; the agent's answer shows how items are listed
옵션에 침대는 없고 에어컨이랑 인덕션만 있어요.
No bed in the options, just AC and an induction stove.
Listing what IS and ISN'T included item by item — essential because 풀옵션 still sometimes means no bed
nuance: 옵션 here is the loanword 'option' used in a Korean-specific real-estate sense: the appliances and furniture that come with the rental — fridge (냉장고), washer (세탁기), air conditioner (에어컨), induction/gas stove (인덕션/가스레인지), bed (침대), desk, wardrobe, etc. 풀옵션 ('full option') means move-in ready with everything; a 'no-option' place is bare. This matters enormously because furnishing a Korean apartment yourself is costly, so 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? is one of the most practical viewing questions. The dividing line from 관리비 is category: 옵션 is the stuff physically INSIDE the unit (appliances, furniture), while 관리비 is the monthly building-management charge — don't conflate them. The English-speaker trap is using 옵션 in its English sense of 'alternatives/choices', which confuses the agent; in housing 옵션 always means built-in appliances and furniture. Particle trap: 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? sets 옵션 as the topic with 은, then asks 뭐'가' 있어요 (subject particle, since 있다 is intransitive) — never say 뭐를 있어요. Even if told '풀옵션', confirm item by item because one essential item (often the bed) can still be missing. Always 존댓말 with the agent.

structuredNuance.t: 옵션은 ('as for the options') + 뭐가 있어요? ('what exists?'). Here 옵션 is a Korean real-estate term meaning the appliances and furniture included with the unit — NOT 'options' in the English sense of 'choices'. 풀옵션 means the unit comes fully equipped; a bare place with no 옵션 means you buy everything yourself.

Ask during any viewing, immediately after the rent/deposit questions. 존댓말 with the agent always. The shorthand 풀옵션이에요? ('is it full-option?') is the fastest way to get the big picture, followed by confirming specific items. 반말 (옵션 뭐 있어?) only with friends.

옵션 (appliances/furniture included with the unit) vs. 관리비 (monthly building management charge) — completely different categories. Don't ask 관리비에 세탁기 포함이에요? — appliances are 옵션, not 관리비. Also 풀옵션 vs. 반옵션: 반옵션 means some but not all basics are included.
풀옵션이에요? (all included?). 에어컨/세탁기/냉장고 있어요? (ask specific items). 옵션 목록 좀 알 수 있어요? (can I get a list?). After viewing: 옵션 중에 나중에 빼 갈 것도 있어요? (will any items be taken when the landlord moves out?).

Two traps: (1) Using 옵션 to mean 'choices/alternatives' — in Korean real estate it means built-in appliances/furniture, not options in the English sense. (2) Particle error: 뭐가 있어요? not 뭐를 있어요 — 있다 takes a subject (이/가), never an object (을/를).

mistakes: Using 옵션 in its general English sense ('choices').
In Korean real estate 옵션 means the included appliances/furniture, not 'alternatives'. 옵션은 뭐가 있어요? asks what the unit comes with, not what your choices are.
Trusting '풀옵션' without checking specifics.
풀옵션 varies by listing and may still lack the item you need (e.g. no bed). Confirm piece by piece: 세탁기 있어요? 침대도 있어요?
Saying 옵션은 뭐를 있어요.
있다 ('to exist') takes a subject, not an object: 옵션은 뭐'가' 있어요? The object particle 를 is wrong with 있다.

usage: Polite; asking the available move-in date
반말, casual 들어가다 ('go in') for moving in
More formal, naming 입주 가능일 ('available date')
Can I move in right away?
Asking if immediate move-in (즉시입주) is possible
examples: 이 집 언제 입주 가능해요?
When can I move into this place?
Pinning down availability on a unit you like — ask this as soon as you're interested, not after you've decided
A: 다음 달 초에 입주하고 싶은데 가능해요? / B: 지금 세입자가 이번 달 말에 나가서 가능해요.
A: I'd like to move in early next month — is that possible? / B: The current tenant leaves at month's end, so yes.
State your target date with 입주하고 싶다; the agent's answer shows the typical timing explanation
지금 사람이 살고 있어서 다음 달에나 입주 가능해요.
Someone's living here now, so move-in's only possible next month.
다음 달에나 ('not until next month') — the 에나 particle signals a reluctant minimum, a nuance worth learning
nuance: 입주 (入住, 'moving in / taking up residence') is the formal real-estate word for occupying a home. 입주 가능해요? asks when the unit is free for you to move in — critical in Korea because the previous tenant's move-out, the deposit hand-over, and the lease start all have to align. 즉시입주 ('immediate move-in') is a common listing tag meaning no waiting period; 바로 입주 돼요? asks for that. The near-synonym 들어가다 ('to go in') is the casual everyday form: 언제 들어갈 수 있어요? — both are natural, but 입주하다 is the proper word on contracts and with agents. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'move in' as 움직이다 ('to physically move/budge') — that verb is wrong for settling into a residence; use 입주하다 for the formal date a place becomes available, and 이사하다 / 이사 오다 for the whole act of relocating. Another trap is 가능하다's conjugation: it combines 가능 + 하다, so it becomes 가능해요, not 가능있어요 (a very common learner error). Also note 에나 in 다음 달에나: this stresses a reluctant minimum ('not before next month at the earliest'), a nuance plain 에 does not carry. Use 존댓말 with the agent.

structuredNuance.t: 입주 (入住) literally means 'entering to reside'. 가능해요? = 'is it possible?'. Together: 'Is it possible to enter/take up residence?' In practice this asks the specific DATE the unit becomes available to move into, which is often constrained by the current tenant's departure or contract timing.

Ask this as soon as a unit interests you — before arranging a viewing is even better. 존댓말 always with the agent. 입주 가능일이 언제예요? is slightly more formal (naming 가능일 as a noun). 반말 (언제 들어갈 수 있어?) only with a friend helping you search.

입주하다 (formal, 'take up residence') vs. 들어가다 (casual, 'go in / move in') vs. 이사하다 ('relocate/move your belongings'). For asking when a unit is available: 입주 가능해요? 바로 입주 돼요? For asking about moving day itself: 이사 언제 해요?

바로 입주 돼요? (immediate move-in?). 즉시입주예요? (same, using the listing term). 입주 가능일이 언제예요? (more formal). 언제 들어갈 수 있어요? (casual spoken). After hearing the date: 그날 바로 이사 와도 돼요? (can I move stuff in that day?).

Three traps: (1) Using 움직이다 ('to budge/move physically') for 'move in' — wrong; use 입주하다 or 들어가다. (2) Saying 가능있어요 — 가능하다 is a 하다 adjective, conjugates to 가능해요. (3) Missing the nuance of 에나 in 다음 달에나 — it means 'not until next month at the earliest', stronger than plain 다음 달에.

mistakes: Translating 'move in' as 움직이다.
움직이다 means to physically move/budge. Moving into a home is 입주하다 (formal) or 들어가다 (casual). Ask 언제 입주 가능해요? or 언제 들어갈 수 있어요?
Saying 입주 가능있어요.
가능하다 is a 하다-adjective: 가능해요, not 가능있어요. Correct: 언제 입주 가능해요? or 입주 가능한가요?
Confusing 입주 with 이사.
입주 is taking up the new residence (and its available date); 이사 is the act of relocating/moving your stuff. For when the place is free, ask 입주 가능해요?; for the moving day itself, 이사 언제 해요?

english: How long is it from the station?
usage: How long does it take from the station?
Polite; asking walking distance to the subway
How many minutes on foot from the station?
Specifies 걸어서 ('on foot') for an exact walk time
Is this near a station (prime location)?
역세권 = the desirable 'within walking distance of a station' zone
examples: 여기 역에서 얼마나 걸려요?
How long is it from the station here?
Standard location question at a viewing; follows naturally after the rent/options check
A: 지하철역에서 걸어서 얼마나 걸려요? / B: 한 십 분 정도 걸려요.
A: How long is the walk from the subway station? / B: About ten minutes.
걸어서 ('on foot') forces a walking answer; 한 ('about') + 십 분 정도 = 'roughly 10 minutes' — the hedged form agents use
역세권이라 좀 비싸도 출퇴근은 편해요.
It's near the station, so it's pricey but the commute's easy.
역세권 justifies higher rent with 출퇴근 ('commute') convenience — if an agent stresses this, expect to pay more
nuance: 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? is 역 ('station') + 에서 ('from', marking the source) + 얼마나 ('how much') + 걸리다 ('to take [time]') + 요. It asks how long the journey from the nearest subway station takes — the single most important location question for commuters in Korea, where subway proximity hugely affects both quality of life and rent. The buzzword 역세권 (驛勢圈, 'station-influence zone') signals a location within easy walking distance; it is a real selling point that pushes prices up. Crucially, 걸리다 here means 'to take time', which is a completely different verb from 걷다 ('to walk') and 걸다 ('to hang/call') — they look and sound similar, a notorious learner trap. Add 걸어서 ('on foot') to pin down a walking answer, since agents might otherwise quote bus or car times. The source particle is 에서 (역에서), not 에 (역에 marks a destination, not origin) — a particle error that mis-marks the direction of travel. Saying 역에서 얼마나 걸어요? ('how do you walk from the station?') wrongly uses 걷다 and asks about the manner of walking, not the duration. Stay in 존댓말 with the agent; you can ask the same about a bus stop: 버스 정류장에서 얼마나 걸려요?

structuredNuance.t: 역(station) + 에서(from) + 얼마나(how much/long) + 걸리다(to take time). Literally 'How much time does it take from the station?' In practice this is the key commute question: proximity to a subway station is the top location factor in Korean renting, and '역세권' (within easy walking distance) is a premium selling point.

Ask at every viewing, after the price and options questions. 존댓말 with the agent. Add 걸어서 ('on foot') when you want the walking time specifically: 역에서 걸어서 얼마나 걸려요? Omitting it leaves the agent free to quote driving or bus time. 반말 (역에서 얼마나 걸려?) only with friends.

걸리다 ('to take time') vs. 걷다 ('to walk') vs. 걸다 ('to hang/dial') — three different verbs that look similar. 역에서 얼마나 걸려요? (걸리다 = time taken) is correct. 역에서 얼마나 걸어요? (걷다) oddly asks 'how do you walk from the station?' — wrong verb for asking duration.
역에서 걸어서 몇 분이에요? (how many minutes on foot?). 여기 역세권이에요? (is it station-zone?). 버스 정류장에서 얼마나 걸려요? (from the bus stop?). 차로는 얼마나 걸려요? (by car?) — use when driving matters to you.

Two traps: (1) Particle: 역'에서' marks the starting point ('from the station'); 역'에' marks a destination — using 에 here flips the direction. (2) Verb confusion: 걸리다 (to take time) ≠ 걷다 (to walk). Saying 역에서 얼마나 걸어요? asks how you walk, not how long it takes.

mistakes: Confusing 걸리다 ('to take time') with 걷다 ('to walk').
역에서 얼마나 걸려요? asks how long it takes. 역에서 얼마나 걸어요? wrongly asks 'how do you walk?'. For walk TIME, keep 걸리다, optionally with 걸어서: 걸어서 얼마나 걸려요?
Using 역에 instead of 역에서.
에 marks a destination; 에서 marks a starting point. From the station, it's 역에서 얼마나 걸려요?. 역에 얼마나 걸려요 mis-marks the source.
Treating 역세권 as just 'near the station' with no cost effect.
역세권 is a value term: it signals desirability and higher rent. If an agent stresses 역세권, expect to pay more for the convenience.

usage: Polite; asking about natural light / direction
채광 = the technical word for natural-light quality
남향 (south-facing) = the most prized, sunniest orientation
examples: 이 방 햇빛 잘 들어요?
Does this room get good sunlight?
Asked while standing in the room at a viewing — the answer often reveals orientation and floor before you even ask
A: 남향이에요? / B: 네, 남향이라 오후에 햇빛 잘 들어요.
A: Does it face south? / B: Yes, it faces south so it gets good afternoon sun.
남향 ('south-facing') is the gold-standard answer; probe floor too — even south-facing units on low floors can be shaded
반지하라 햇빛이 잘 안 들어서 좀 어두워요.
It's a semi-basement, so not much sun gets in — it's a bit dark.
반지하 ('semi-basement') is the biggest warning sign for poor light; 어둡다 = dark — factor this into 관리비 if heating covers a dark unit
nuance: 햇빛 잘 들어요? is 햇빛 ('sunlight') + 잘 ('well') + 들다 ('to enter/come in') + 요, literally 'does sunlight come in well?' — asking whether the unit gets good natural light. In Korea this matters enormously: good sun affects mood, mold prevention, heating bills, and resale value. The verb 들다 here means 'to enter/be admitted' (light coming in), NOT 'to hold' or 'to lift' — 햇빛이 들다 is a fixed collocation. The technical term is 채광 (採光, 'natural-light intake'); 채광 좋아요? is how professionals phrase it. Direction language is crucial: 남향 (south-facing) is the gold standard, 동향 (east) gets morning sun, 서향 (west) gets afternoon, and 북향 (north-facing) and 반지하 (semi-basement) units often have chronic darkness and damp. The English-speaker trap is the verb: '직역-ing 'gets sunlight' as 햇빛 가져요? or 햇빛 있어요? is meaningless; the natural collocation is 햇빛이 들다. Another is the particle: 햇빛이 잘 들어요? uses subject 이 (햇빛 is what comes in), never object 을. After asking about light, probe 곰팡이 안 생겨요? ('does mold not grow here?') to check for damp — dark, poorly lit units are mold risks. Always 존댓말 at viewings.

structuredNuance.t: 햇빛('sunlight') + 잘('well') + 들다('to enter/come in'). Literally 'does sunlight come in well?' The verb 들다 here means light entering the space — a fixed collocation. This is NOT 햇빛을 받아요? ('do you receive sunlight?') or 햇빛 있어요? — Korean talks about light 'coming in' (들다), not 'being present'.

Ask while standing in the unit, ideally checking by looking at the windows and their direction. 존댓말 with the agent. 채광 좋아요? is slightly more technical and sounds knowledgeable. 반말 (햇빛 잘 들어?) only with a friend. Follow up with 남향이에요? and 곰팡이 안 생겨요? for a full picture.

햇빛 잘 들어요? (everyday) vs. 채광 좋아요? (technical/professional). Direction terms: 남향 (south, sunniest) > 동향 (east, morning sun) > 서향 (west, afternoon) > 북향 (north, least sun). 반지하 (semi-basement) means poor light regardless of direction.
채광 좋아요? (pro version). 남향이에요? (direct direction check). 햇빛이 오래 들어요? ('does sun stay long?'). 반지하예요? (is it semi-basement?). 곰팡이 안 생겨요? (probe mold — follows naturally from a light/damp concern).

Two traps: (1) Verb choice: 햇빛 가져요?/있어요? are unnatural — the correct collocation is 햇빛이 들다 ('light comes in'). (2) Particle: 햇빛'이' 잘 들어요? — 들다 (to come in) is intransitive, so 햇빛 is the subject (이/가), never the object (을). Saying 햇빛을 잘 들어요 is wrong.

mistakes: Saying 햇빛 가져요? or 햇빛 있어요? for 'gets sunlight'.
The natural collocation is 햇빛이 들다 ('light comes in'). Ask 햇빛 잘 들어요?. 가지다 ('to have') and a bare 있다 don't fit how Korean talks about sun exposure.
Using the object particle: 햇빛을 잘 들어요.
들다 ('to come in') is intransitive here, so 햇빛 is the subject: 햇빛이 잘 들어요?. The object marker 을 is wrong.
Ignoring 남향/북향 and 반지하.
Direction and floor decide the light. 남향 (south-facing) is sunny; 북향 and 반지하 (semi-basement) are often dark. If sun matters, confirm 남향이에요? and avoid surprises.

english: Could you lower the rent a bit?
usage: Please lower the rent a bit
반말, only with a friend, never the landlord
월세 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요?
Couldn't you take just a little off the rent?
Softer, more pleading 'wouldn't it be okay if…'
At least waive some of the maintenance fee
Fallback: ask to cut 관리비 if rent won't budge
examples: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요. 오만 원만요.
Please lower the rent a bit — just 50,000 off.
Name a concrete cut (오만 원만요 = 'just 50k') to make the ask specific and easier for the landlord to agree to
A: 계약 바로 할 테니까 월세 좀 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? / B: 오만 원은 빼 드릴게요.
A: I'll sign right away, so couldn't you lower the rent a little? / B: I can take off 50,000.
Offering to commit immediately (계약 바로) as leverage is the most common negotiation tactic — the B response shows what acceptance looks like
보증금 더 낼 테니까 월세 좀 깎아 주세요.
I'll pay more deposit, so please lower the monthly rent.
The 보증금↑ → 월세↓ trade stated as a bargaining chip — the landlord keeps the risk-benefit of a larger deposit
nuance: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 is 월세 ('monthly rent') + 좀 (softener that turns the request polite, not 'a little' in amount) + 깎다 ('to cut/shave down a price') + 아 주세요 ('please do for me'). 깎다 is THE price-cutting verb in Korean — used at markets, restaurants, and real estate alike; it's the right word here. Rent negotiation is normal in Korea, especially on 월세 and 관리비, and landlords expect some back-and-forth. To make the ask more effective, name an exact amount (오만 원만요) and offer something in return: signing immediately (계약 바로 할게요) or raising the deposit (보증금 더 낼게요). The dividing line from 보증금 깎아 주세요 is which financial lever you're pulling — you can negotiate the deposit down OR the monthly up and the deposit up; both are valid. The English-speaker trap is using 내리다 ('to bring something down physically') instead of 깎다 — 월세 내려 주세요 is understandable but sounds like lowering an object, not cutting a price. Another trap is 할인해 주세요 ('give me a discount') — 할인 fits stores and sales promotions, not rent haggling. Bargaining hard while staying 존댓말 is expected and respected; 반말 with a landlord or agent would torpedo the deal.

structuredNuance.t: 월세 + 좀 (softener) + 깎다 (to shave/cut a price) + 아 주세요 (please do for me). Literally 'please shave the monthly rent a bit'. 깎다 is the dedicated Korean price-cutting verb — used for any price negotiation, not just housing. The 좀 is a politeness softener, NOT a quantity limiter; you specify the actual cut separately (오만 원만요).

Use after you've decided on a unit but before signing. Always 존댓말 — this is a business negotiation. Pair the ask with leverage: 계약 바로 할게요 (I'll sign now) or 보증금 더 낼게요 (I'll raise the deposit). The softer form 월세 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? is more pleading and appropriate if the landlord seems firm.

깎다 (cut a price, the right verb) vs. 내리다 (lower physically, wrong for prices) vs. 할인하다 (discount, fits stores not rent). Negotiation levers: 월세 깎아 주세요 (lower the monthly) vs. 보증금 깎아 주세요 (lower the deposit) vs. 관리비 빼 주세요 (waive some maintenance) — choose the lever that makes sense.

월세 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? (softer, more pleading). 관리비라도 좀 빼 주세요 (fallback: at least cut the maintenance fee). 오만 원만 깎아 주세요 (name the exact cut). 보증금 더 낼 테니까 월세 깎아 주세요 (trade: raise deposit for lower rent).

Two traps: (1) Using 내리다 instead of 깎다 — 월세 내려 주세요 sounds like lowering an object; for shaving a price use 깎다. (2) Using 할인해 주세요 — 할인 is for store/sales discounts, not rent. In rent negotiation, 깎다 is the only natural verb.

mistakes: Saying 월세 내려 주세요 for 'lower the rent'.
내리다 is to physically lower/bring down. For shaving money off a price, Koreans use 깎다: 월세 좀 깎아 주세요. 내리다 sounds like lowering an object.
Using 할인해 주세요 to haggle rent.
할인 (discount) fits stores and sales, not rent negotiation. For bargaining down rent, say 깎아 주세요. 할인해 주세요 sounds like asking a shop for a coupon.
Dropping 좀 and demanding 월세 깎아 주세요 flatly.
Without the softener 좀 it sounds pushy. 월세 좀 깎아 주세요 is polite; pair it with leverage (보증금 더 낼게요 / 계약 바로 할게요) to negotiate gracefully.

hangul: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요?
english: Can I look around a bit more?
usage: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요?
Can I look around a bit more?
Polite; asking for more time to inspect the unit
Can I look a bit more?
반말, with a friend who came along
Could I take my time looking?
Softer, asks to view at your own pace
Please show me other places too
Asking to see additional units beyond this one
examples: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? 화장실도 보고 싶어서요.
Can I look around a bit more? I'd like to see the bathroom too.
Give a reason (화장실도 보고 싶다) to extend the viewing — it sounds more natural and the agent is more likely to give you time
A: 수압이랑 옵션 좀 천천히 볼 수 있을까요? / B: 네, 천천히 보세요.
A: Could I take my time checking the water pressure and appliances? / B: Sure, take your time.
Name what to inspect (수압, 옵션) so the agent understands; 천천히 볼 수 있을까요? is softer than 볼 수 있어요?
이 집은 좀 그렇고, 다른 집도 보여 주세요.
This one's not quite it — please show me others too.
좀 그렇다 ('a bit meh/not quite right') politely declines without a harsh 싫어요 — the standard soft rejection before asking for more
nuance: 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is 여기 ('here') + 좀 ('a bit', softener) + 더 ('more') + 볼 수 있어요 ('can I see?'), asking the agent for more time to inspect a unit — check closets, test 수압 ('water pressure'), look for 곰팡이 ('mold'), count the outlets. Korean viewings can feel rushed because agents juggle many clients, so this phrase buys you the time to look properly. The critical distinction is 보다 ('to see/inspect', what YOU do) vs. 보여 주다 ('to show', what the AGENT does): 여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? means you want to keep looking yourself; 더 보여 주세요 means you want the agent to show you more. Don't say 여기 좀 더 보여 줄 수 있어요? when you just want to linger — that asks the agent to show you, not for you to inspect at your own pace. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'look around' as 둘러보다 — fine but slightly stiffer; 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? is the more natural spoken ask. To reject a place without being rude, Koreans say 좀 그렇네요 / 좀 별로예요 rather than a blunt 싫어요. Stay in 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: 여기('here') + 좀('a bit') + 더('more') + 볼 수 있어요?('can I see?'). Literally 'can I see here a bit more?' — asking for extra time to inspect the unit yourself. The key verb is 보다 (you inspect), NOT 보여 주다 (agent shows you). If you want to keep looking yourself, this is the phrase; if you want the agent to show you something, say 보여 주세요.

Use mid-viewing when you feel rushed or want to check something specific (수압, 곰팡이, outlets, closets). 존댓말 with the agent always. The softer 천천히 좀 봐도 될까요? is better when you want to set your own pace entirely. 반말 (좀 더 봐도 돼?) only with a friend who came along.

볼 수 있어요? (you look more, THIS unit) vs. 다른 집도 보여 주세요 (agent shows MORE units). These are different requests — confusing them either cuts your inspection short or skips ahead to different places. Use the right one depending on whether you want more time here or want to move on.
천천히 좀 봐도 될까요? (softer, own-pace version). 좀 더 둘러봐도 돼요? (slightly more formal 둘러보다). 화장실/부엌도 볼 수 있어요? (request a specific room). 이 집은 좀 그렇고, 다른 집 보여 주세요 (politely move on).

Two traps: (1) Saying 여기 좀 더 보여 줄 수 있어요? when you want to keep inspecting yourself — 보여 주다 asks the agent to show you, not for you to linger. Use 볼 수 있어요? for your own inspection. (2) Rejecting a place with 이 집 싫어요 — too blunt; soften with 좀 그렇네요 / 좀 별로예요.

mistakes: Saying 여기 좀 더 보여 줄 수 있어요? when you want to keep looking yourself.
보여 주다 means the agent shows it to you. To keep inspecting on your own, say 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? (you see it). Use 보여 주세요 only when asking them to show something.
Confusing 'look around more' with 'show me other places'.
여기 좀 더 볼 수 있어요? extends this viewing; 다른 집도 보여 주세요 asks for additional units. Say the one you mean, or the agent stops at this one or skips ahead.
Bluntly saying 이 집 싫어요 to reject a place.
A flat 싫어요 sounds harsh to an agent. Koreans soften with 좀 그렇네요 / 좀 별로예요 ('it's kind of meh') before asking 다른 집도 보여 주세요.

usage: Polite; deciding on the unit you want
반말, with a friend confirming a choice
I'd like to take this place
Softer, stating preference before fully committing
More committal: moving straight to signing a contract
examples: 여기 마음에 들어요. 이 집으로 할게요.
I like it here. I'll take this place.
마음에 들다 ('to like/be pleased with') leads naturally into the decision — note the fixed particle 에 in 마음에 들다, not 마음을
A: 고민해 봤는데 그냥 이 집으로 할게요. / B: 그러시면 바로 계약 진행할까요?
A: I thought it over and I'll just go with this place. / B: In that case, shall we proceed with the contract right away?
고민해 봤다 ('thought it over') shows you weighed it; the agent's response shows what comes next — the 계약 process
이 집으로 할게요. 계약은 언제 할 수 있어요?
I'll take this one. When can we do the contract?
Decide, then move to scheduling 계약 — this two-step sequence is the natural flow
nuance: 이 집으로 할게요 is 이 집 ('this house') + -으로 ('with/via', marking the chosen option) + 하다 ('to do/go with') + -ㄹ게요 (announcing your own decision politely). The -으로 + 하다 construction means 'I'll go with this one among the options' — the same pattern as ordering at a restaurant (이걸로 할게요), here applied to choosing a home. The -ㄹ게요 ending courteously declares YOUR resolve ('I'll do it'); it differs from -ㄹ게요's sibling -ㄹ까요 ('shall we?'), which is a suggestion. The dividing line from 이 집 계약할게요 is finality: 이 집으로 할게요 announces your CHOICE; 계약하다 commits to the legal CONTRACT. In natural flow you say 이 집으로 할게요 first, then arrange the 계약. The particle -으로 carries the 'selecting from among options' nuance — dropping it (이 집 할게요) is understandable but loses that sense. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'I'll take it' as 가질게요 ('I'll possess it') or 잡을게요 ('I'll grab it') — both wrong; for choosing a rental you use 이 집으로 하다 (select) then 계약하다 (commit). Also: 마음에 들다 ('to like') is a fixed expression with the locative particle 에: 이 집이 마음에 들어요 — never 마음을 들어요. Stay in 존댓말 as you close.

structuredNuance.t: 이 집(-으로) + 하다 + -ㄹ게요. 이 집으로 하다 literally means 'to do it as/with this house' — the -으로 housemarks the chosen option, like ordering (이걸로 할게요). -ㄹ게요 announces your own decision. The real meaning: 'I'm going with this one' among the options the agent showed you.

Use this the moment you've decided on a unit, before arranging the 계약. Always 존댓말 with the agent — this is the pivotal close of a business transaction. The softer 이 집으로 하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to go with this one') works when you're interested but not 100% committed yet. 반말 (이걸로 할게) only with friends.

이 집으로 할게요 (announces choice) → then 계약할게요 (commits to the legal contract). These are sequential steps, not synonyms. 이 집으로 하고 싶어요 is softer and less committed — use it if you still need to confirm something before deciding.
이 집으로 하고 싶어요 (softer: I'd like this one). 이 집 계약할게요 (more committal: I'll sign). 고민해 봤는데 이 집으로 할게요 (after deliberating). 여기 마음에 들어요, 이 집으로 할게요 (liking + decision).

Two traps: (1) Translating 'I'll take it' as 가질게요/잡을게요 — you don't 'possess' or 'grab' a rental; for choosing use 이 집으로 하다, for signing use 계약하다. (2) Mangling 마음에 들다: it's 마음'에' 들다 (fixed locative 에), not 마음'을' 들다. 이 집이 마음에 들어요 = I like this place.

mistakes: Saying 이 집 가질게요 to mean 'I'll take it'.
가지다 ('to possess') doesn't fit choosing a rental. To pick this unit, say 이 집으로 할게요; to commit legally, 이 집 계약할게요.
Dropping -으로: 이 집 할게요.
The -으로 marks 'going with this choice'. 이 집으로 할게요 cleanly says 'I'll go with this one'; without it the 'among options' nuance is lost.
Mangling 마음에 들다 as 마음을 들어요.
It's a fixed phrase with 에: 이 집이 마음에 들어요 ('I like this place'). The object particle 을 is wrong here.

usage: Polite; asking the agent to walk you through it
How do we do the contract?
반말, with a friend who knows the ropes
What do I need to sign the contract?
Asking what documents/money are required (신분증 등)
How much is the down payment?
계약금 = the deposit-on-signing that locks the deal
examples: 이 집으로 할게요. 계약은 어떻게 해요?
I'll take this place. How does the contract work?
Decide first with 이 집으로 할게요, then ask how to proceed — this is the natural two-step sequence
A: 계약할 때 신분증이랑 뭐 필요해요? / B: 신분증이랑 도장이랑 계약금 가져오시면 돼요.
A: What do I need to bring to sign — ID and what else? / B: Just bring your ID, seal/stamp, and the down payment.
The agent's answer shows the three standard items: 신분증 (ID), 도장 (personal seal), 계약금 (down payment) — know all three before the signing day
오늘 계약금 걸고 잔금은 입주할 때 내면 돼요.
Pay the down payment today, and the balance when you move in.
계약금 (down) now, 잔금 ('balance/remainder') at 입주 — this two-payment split is the standard pattern
nuance: 계약 (契約, 'contract') is the legal rental agreement, and 계약은 어떻게 해요? asks the agent to explain how signing works — what you bring, what you pay, and in what sequence. The key vocabulary clusters here: 계약금 (the down payment at signing, typically around 10% of the total deposit, which locks the deal and makes it binding on both sides), 잔금 ('the balance', paid at move-in), and 도장 (personal seal/stamp, often used in Korea instead of a signature). The dividing line from 보증금 is timing and role: 계약금 is a partial payment at signing that secures the contract; 보증금 is the full security deposit, of which 계약금 is the first installment. Critically, newcomers must ask about 전입신고 ('move-in registration') and 확정일자 ('fixed date stamp') — two official steps that legally protect your deposit from being lost if the landlord defaults; skipping them can leave your money unprotected. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'sign a contract' as 사인하다 — while colloquially understood, the proper term is 계약하다, and Koreans often 도장 (stamp) rather than sign. The topic particle 은 in 계약은 어떻게 해요? topicalizes 계약 ('as for the contract…') and is the natural form. Always 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: 계약(contract) + 은(topic) + 어떻게(how) + 해요?(do we do?). Literally 'how do we do the contract?' — asking the agent to explain the entire signing process: what to bring, what to pay, and the order of steps. It's the natural question after 이 집으로 할게요.

Use immediately after deciding on a unit. 존댓말 always — this is a legal transaction. Ask 계약하려면 뭐가 필요해요? if you want a checklist of requirements. 반말 (계약 어떻게 해?) only with a friend who has rented before and can explain the process to you.

계약금 vs. 보증금: 계약금 is the partial down payment at signing (locks the deal); 보증금 is the full security deposit — 계약금 is typically the first installment of the 보증금. 잔금 ('balance') = the rest, paid at move-in. These three terms form the payment sequence: 계약금 → 잔금 → done.
계약하려면 뭐가 필요해요? (what do I need?). 계약금은 얼마예요? (how much is the down payment?). 전입신고랑 확정일자는 어떻게 해요? (essential follow-up for deposit protection). 계약서 한번 읽어봐도 돼요? (can I read the contract first?).

Two traps: (1) Saying 사인할게요 for 'I'll sign' — colloquially understood but the proper verb is 계약하다; Koreans often stamp (도장) rather than sign. (2) Skipping 전입신고 and 확정일자 — these legally protect your deposit; neglecting them can leave your 보증금 unprotected if the landlord defaults.

mistakes: Confusing 계약금 with 보증금.
계약금 is the down payment at signing that locks the deal (part of the total); 보증금 is the full security deposit. You usually pay 계약금 now and the 잔금 (balance) at move-in.
Saying only 사인할게요 for signing a contract.
사인 (autograph) is colloquial; the proper verb is 계약하다, and Koreans often use a 도장 (seal/stamp). Say 계약할게요 for committing to the lease.
Skipping 전입신고 and 확정일자.
These official move-in registration steps legally protect your deposit. Ask the agent 전입신고랑 확정일자 어떻게 해요? — neglecting them can leave your 보증금 unprotected.

usage: Polite; a key 'check before you sign' question
반말, with a friend at the viewing
Does the hot water come out well?
온수 ('hot water') — vital in winter; 잘 나오다 = flows well
Doesn't it get cold in winter?
Probing insulation/heating (난방) for the cold months
examples: 여기 수압은 괜찮아요? 좀 약한 거 같아서요.
Is the water pressure okay here? It seems a bit weak.
약하다 ('weak') voices the worry directly — this is the natural way to flag a concern while still asking politely
A: 온수도 잘 나오고 수압도 괜찮아요? / B: 네, 문제없어요. 도시가스라서요.
A: Does the hot water run well and is the pressure okay too? / B: Yes, no problem — it's city gas.
Bundle 온수 + 수압 in one ask; the agent's mention of 도시가스 (city gas) is useful for estimating your winter heating bills
꼭대기 층이라 수압이 좀 약할 수 있어요.
It's the top floor, so the water pressure might be a bit weak.
꼭대기 층 ('top floor') is a red flag for weak 수압 — a fact to know before viewing high floors
nuance: 수압은 괜찮아요? is 수압 (水壓, 'water pressure') + 은 (topic) + 괜찮아요? ('is it okay?'), one of those practical questions that separates a savvy renter from a regretful one — weak pressure or cold showers are misery you only discover after moving in. Pair it with 온수 잘 나와요? ('does hot water come out well?') and 겨울에 안 추워요? ('isn't it cold in winter?') for a full practical inspection. The natural collocation for water/heat flowing is 나오다 ('to come out'): 물이 잘 나와요, 온수가 잘 나와요, 냉수가 잘 나와요. The dividing line from 난방 ('heating') is system: 수압/온수 concerns water flow through pipes, while 난방 concerns warmth — Korean homes commonly use 온돌 (under-floor radiant heating), and the fuel source (도시가스 vs. other) significantly affects your monthly bill, so ask 난방 어떻게 해요? too. Top floors (꼭대기 층) and old buildings often have weak 수압 — knowing this helps you ask before you fall in love with a unit. The English-speaker trap is the particle on 나오다: water is the SUBJECT coming out (물'이' 잘 나와요?), never the object — 나오다 is intransitive. Another is asking 물이 세요? ('is the water forceful/violent?') — the adjective 세다 can be used colloquially for strong pressure, but 수압 괜찮아요? is the cleaner and more natural form. Stay in 존댓말 at the viewing.

structuredNuance.t: 수압(水壓, 'water pressure') + 은(topic) + 괜찮아요?(is it okay?). Literally 'Is the water pressure okay?' In real terms this is a proxy question for daily livability: weak pressure means bad showers and slow taps. Top floors and old buildings are notorious for poor 수압 — this question can surface a real hidden problem.

Ask while standing in the bathroom during any viewing — ideally turn the tap on and check yourself rather than relying on the agent's word. 존댓말 always. Pair immediately with 온수 잘 나와요? and 겨울에 안 추워요? for a complete comfort check. 반말 (수압 괜찮아?) only with friends.

수압/온수 (water pressure and hot water) vs. 난방 (heating): different systems. 수압 괜찮아요? probes the pipes; 겨울에 안 추워요? / 난방 어떻게 해요? probes the heating. Ask both. Also 도시가스 vs. 전기 vs. 기름 보일러 — the heat source changes your monthly bill significantly.

온수 잘 나와요? (hot water check). 겨울에 안 추워요? (heating/insulation check). 난방 어떻게 해요? (what heating system?). 수압이 좀 약한 것 같아요 (stating rather than asking, if you've already tried it). 꼭대기 층이라 수압이 괜찮을까요? (ask before seeing top-floor units).

Two traps: (1) Particle: water is the subject coming out — 물'이' 잘 나와요? (이/가), never 물'을'. 나오다 ('to come out') is intransitive. (2) Only checking pressure and forgetting 온수 and 난방 — weak hot water or poor insulation each ruin daily life just as badly as weak pressure.

mistakes: Saying 물을 잘 나와요? with the object particle.
나오다 ('to come out') is intransitive; the water is the subject: 물이 잘 나와요?, 온수가 잘 나와요?. The object marker 을 is wrong.
Only checking pressure and forgetting 온수 and 난방.
Weak 수압, no 온수 (hot water), or poor 난방 (heating) each ruin daily life. Ask 수압 괜찮아요?, 온수 잘 나와요?, and 겨울에 안 추워요? together.
Not asking what heating type it is.
Bills depend on it. Ask 난방 어떻게 해요? — 도시가스 (city gas) vs. other systems changes your winter costs a lot. 온돌 (floor heating) is common but cost varies by source.

english: How long is the lease term?
usage: How long is the lease term?
Polite; asking the length of the contract
How many years is a typical contract?
Asking the standard term (often 2년 for 전세)
재계약 = renewing/extending when the term ends
examples: 보통 계약 기간은 얼마예요? 일 년이에요, 이 년이에요?
How long's the usual lease — one year or two?
Offering the two common terms (일 년, 이 년) makes the answer easy for the agent — and shows you know the Korean norm
A: 일 년 계약하고 싶은데 가능해요? / B: 집주인분이 이 년을 원하시는데 협의는 가능해요.
A: I'd like a one-year contract — is that possible? / B: The landlord wants two years, but it's negotiable.
State your preferred term with 계약하고 싶다; the agent's answer shows the landlord's preference and whether there's room to negotiate
이 년 계약이고, 만기 때 재계약하면 돼요.
It's a two-year lease, and you can renew at the end.
만기 ('expiry of term') + 재계약 ('renewal') — what happens when the contract runs out
nuance: 계약 기간은 얼마예요? is 계약 ('contract') + 기간 (期間, 'period/term') + 은 (topic) + 얼마예요? ('how long/much?'), asking the length of the lease — crucial because it determines how long you are committed and when the landlord can propose a rent increase. The Korean default is 2년 (two years) for most rentals, especially 전세; 월세 can sometimes be 1년. Under Korean tenant-protection law, tenants can request one renewal at the same conditions, making the practical stay potentially 4 years. The verb pairs naturally: 이 년 계약하다 ('sign for two years'). The dividing line from 재계약 (再契約, 'renewal') is timing: 계약 기간 is the original term; 재계약 is extending at 만기 (滿期, 'expiry') — ask both to understand your options from day one. The English-speaker trap is using 얼마예요? and worrying it only means money — it naturally covers duration too, so 계약 기간은 얼마예요? is correct Korean. A separate learner trap is the numeral system for years: Korean years always take Sino-Korean numbers (일 년, 이 년, 삼 년), never native Korean numbers (한 년 is wrong and sounds strange). Stay in 존댓말 with the agent.

structuredNuance.t: 계약(contract) + 기간(期間, term/period) + 은(topic) + 얼마예요?(how long?). Literally 'how long is the contract term?' In practice this question controls your whole timeline: it determines when you can leave, when the landlord can raise rent, and how tenant-protection law applies to you.

Ask this when you're seriously interested in a unit, before signing. 존댓말 always. The variant 보통 몇 년 계약해요? ('how many years is typical?') is useful if you're new to Korean renting and want to understand the norm. 반말 (계약 기간 얼마야?) only with friends.

계약 기간 (original term length) vs. 재계약 (renewal at expiry, 再契約) vs. 만기 (end of term, 滿期). Ask 계약 기간은 얼마예요? for the term, 재계약 돼요? for renewal rights. They are sequential stages of the same lease, not the same question.
보통 몇 년 계약해요? (how many years is standard?). 재계약도 돼요? (can I renew?). 만기 때 월세 올릴 수 있어요? (can rent go up at expiry?). 계약 기간이 어떻게 돼요? (softer phrasing).

Two traps: (1) Thinking 얼마예요? only asks about money — it also asks about duration, so 계약 기간은 얼마예요? is correct Korean for 'how long is the term?'. (2) Using native Korean numbers for years: 한 년, 두 년 are wrong — years always take Sino-Korean numbers: 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년.

mistakes: Saying 한 년, 두 년 for years.
Years take Sino-Korean numbers: 일 년, 이 년, 삼 년 — never 한 년/두 년. So 'a two-year lease' is 이 년 계약, not 두 년 계약.
Thinking 얼마예요? can't ask about duration.
얼마 covers 'how much/how long'. 계약 기간은 얼마예요? correctly asks the lease length. You can also say 계약 기간이 어떻게 돼요?
Confusing 계약 기간 with 재계약.
계약 기간 is the original term length; 재계약 is renewing at expiry (만기). Ask 계약 기간은 얼마예요? for the term and 재계약 돼요? for renewal rights — they're different questions.

usage: Is it kind of noisy here?
Polite; checking the noise level of the place
반말, with a friend at the viewing
Is there bad noise from upstairs?
층간소음 = inter-floor noise, a notorious Korean issue
examples: 여기 밤에 좀 시끄러워요?
Does it get noisy here at night?
밤에 ('at night') targets when noise matters most — daytime viewings are often deceptively quiet
A: 벽이 얇아서 옆집 소리 들려요? / B: 방음이 꽤 잘 돼서 거의 안 들려요.
A: Are the walls thin — can you hear the neighbors? / B: The soundproofing is pretty good, you can barely hear them.
벽이 얇다 ('thin walls') + 소리 들리다 probes 방음 concretely; the B response shows how agents reassure you
큰길 쪽이라 차 소리가 좀 나는데 방음은 괜찮아요.
It faces the main road so there's some car noise, but soundproofing's fine.
Weighing 차 소리 (traffic noise) against decent 방음 — a candid agent answer worth knowing before you decide
nuance: 여기 좀 시끄러워요? is 여기 ('here') + 좀 (softener, 'kind of') + 시끄럽다 ('to be noisy') + 요. The 좀 is essential: without it the question sounds like a complaint rather than an inquiry. 시끄럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective — the ㅂ becomes 워 in all -아/어 conjugations: 시끄럽다 → 시끄러워요, 시끄러웠어요. 층간소음 (層間騷音, 'inter-floor noise') is a notorious and legally contentious issue in Korean apartment life — noise from upstairs neighbors is a common source of disputes. The professional term 방음 (防音, 'soundproofing') asks about the building's structural defense against noise. The dividing line between 소리 and 소음: 소리 is neutral 'sound' (차 소리, 옆집 소리), while 소음 is specifically unwanted 'noise' (층간소음, 소음이 심하다) — use 소음 for the nuisance sense. A quiet afternoon viewing hides night noise, traffic peaks, and upstairs stomping, so probe specifically with 밤에 시끄러워요? and 층간소음 심해요?. The English-speaker trap is the irregular conjugation — saying 시끄럽어요 instead of 시끄러워요. Stay in 존댓말 at the viewing.

structuredNuance.t: 여기('here') + 좀('kind of', softener) + 시끄럽다('to be noisy') + 요. Literally 'is it kind of noisy here?' The 좀 turns the question from a complaint into a polite inquiry. In real terms you're checking for traffic noise, thin walls, and the notorious Korean apartment problem of 층간소음 (noise between floors).

Ask at viewings — ideally at different times of day if possible. 존댓말 with the agent. Probe specifically: 밤에 시끄러워요? (at night?), 층간소음 심해요? (upstairs noise?), 방음 잘 돼요? (soundproofing?). A daytime viewing alone won't reveal noise problems. 반말 (여기 시끄러워?) only with friends.

시끄럽다 (the experienced noise, 'it's loud') vs. 방음 (the structural defense, 'soundproofing') — ask both. Also 소리 (neutral 'sound': 차 소리, 옆집 소리) vs. 소음 (unwanted 'noise': 층간소음, 소음이 심하다) — use 소음 when you mean the nuisance kind.
방음 잘 돼요? (soundproofing?). 층간소음 심해요? (upstairs noise serious?). 밤에 시끄러워요? (at night?). 벽이 얇아요? (are the walls thin?). 큰길이랑 얼마나 가까워요? (how close to the main road?).

Two traps: (1) The ㅂ-irregular: 시끄럽다 → 시끄러워요, NOT 시끄럽어요. The ㅂ becomes 워 before -아/어 endings. (2) Forgetting 좀 — a bare 여기 시끄러워요? without 좀 can sound like a complaint; the softener keeps it a genuine inquiry.

mistakes: Saying 시끄럽어요 instead of 시끄러워요.
시끄럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the ㅂ becomes 워 → 시끄러워요. 시끄럽어요 is the wrong, regular-looking form.
Mixing up 소리 and 소음.
소리 is neutral 'sound' (차 소리, 옆집 소리); 소음 is unwanted 'noise' (층간소음, 소음이 심하다). For complaints about noise, use 소음.
Trusting a quiet daytime viewing.
Noise often peaks at night or from upstairs. Ask 밤에 시끄러워요?, 방음 잘 돼요?, and 층간소음 심해요? — a calm afternoon visit won't reveal them.

english: Is there a loan/mortgage on it?
usage: Is there a loan on it, by any chance?
Polite; a crucial check before paying a deposit
Is there a loan on it?
반말, with a friend helping you vet a place
Is there a mortgage lien on it?
근저당 = the registered lien; the precise legal term
Can I see the property register?
등기부등본 = the official deed/register that shows liens
examples: 혹시 이 집 융자 있어요?
Does this place happen to have a loan on it?
혹시 ('by any chance') softens a sensitive question so it sounds like due diligence, not an accusation — always use it
A: 보증금 넣기 전에 등기부등본이랑 융자 확인하고 싶어요. / B: 네, 제가 출력해 드릴게요.
A: Before I put down the deposit, I want to check the register and any loan. / B: Sure, I'll print it out for you.
보증금 넣기 전에 ('before depositing') is exactly the right time — agents expect this request and a trustworthy agent will readily provide it
근저당이 많이 잡혀 있으면 보증금 떼일 수도 있어요.
If there are big liens, you could lose your deposit.
떼이다 ('to be cheated out of / to lose') — knowing this word helps you understand the real risk this question guards against
nuance: 혹시 융자 있어요? is 혹시 ('by any chance', a softener for delicate questions) + 융자 (融資, 'a loan') + 있어요? ('is there?'), asking whether the property carries debt. If the landlord has borrowed heavily against the home and defaults, a foreclosure auction can swallow a tenant's 보증금 entirely — this is one of the most financially consequential questions a renter can ask in Korea. The specific phenomenon 깡통전세 ('empty-can jeonse') and 전세사기 ('jeonse fraud') describe situations where the deposit equals or exceeds the home's safe value, leaving tenants with nothing. The precise legal term is 근저당 (根抵當, 'maximum-amount mortgage lien'), visible on the 등기부등본 (登記簿謄本, 'certified copy of the property register'), which you have every right to request. The dividing line: 융자/대출 is the loan itself; 근저당 is its registered encumbrance on the title; 등기부등본 is the document that proves both. The English-speaker trap is not knowing to ask at all — the concept of a tenant's deposit being wiped out by the landlord's private debt is foreign to most Western renting experiences. 혹시 is non-negotiable here: a bare 빚 있어요? ('do you have debts?') sounds accusatory and personal; 혹시 융자 있어요? frames it as routine due diligence. Always 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: 혹시('by any chance') + 융자(融資, 'loan/financing') + 있어요?('is there?'). Literally 'Is there a loan on it, by any chance?' The real meaning: 'Is my deposit at risk of being lost if this landlord defaults?' This is one of the most important financial self-protection questions in Korean renting.

Ask BEFORE handing over any money — ideally at the viewing or contract stage. 존댓말 always. Follow up with 등기부등본 좀 볼 수 있어요? — seeing the document yourself is the only reliable verification. A reputable agent will not be offended; reluctance to show the 등기부등본 is itself a red flag.

융자/대출 (the loan) vs. 근저당 (the registered lien on the property, 根抵當) vs. 등기부등본 (the official register showing all encumbrances). These are three layers of the same issue: 혹시 융자 있어요? opens the conversation; 근저당 잡혀 있어요? asks for the legal specifics; 등기부등본 좀 볼 수 있어요? demands proof.

근저당 잡혀 있어요? (technical follow-up). 등기부등본 좀 볼 수 있어요? (request the document). 깡통전세 위험은 없죠? (is there no empty-can jeonse risk?). 전세보증보험 가입 가능한 집이에요? (is the place eligible for jeonse deposit insurance?).

Two traps: (1) Not asking at all — in many Western countries the landlord's personal debt does not threaten the tenant's deposit; in Korea it can, so this question is essential. (2) Dropping 혹시 — 빚 있어요? ('do you have debts?') sounds personal and accusatory; 혹시 융자 있어요? frames it as routine due diligence.

mistakes: Not asking about debt at all before paying the deposit.
If the landlord defaults on a loan, foreclosure can swallow your 보증금. Always ask 혹시 융자 있어요? and check the 등기부등본 before handing over money.
Confusing 융자/근저당/등기부등본.
융자 (or 대출) is the loan; 근저당 is its registered lien on the property; 등기부등본 is the official register showing them. Ask to SEE the 등기부등본 to confirm the 근저당 status.
Asking bluntly without 혹시.
Debt is a sensitive topic. 혹시 융자 있어요? softens it to a routine check. A flat 빚 있어요? ('do you have debts?') sounds personal and accusatory.

english: Can I talk to the landlord directly?
usage: Can I speak with the landlord directly?
Polite; asking to deal with the owner, not just the agent
Can I talk to the landlord directly?
Honorific 분, politely sizing up the owner
Does the landlord live in the same building?
Practical: an on-site owner means faster repairs
examples: 계약 전에 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요?
Before signing, can I speak with the landlord directly?
계약 전에 ('before the contract') is the right moment — verify the owner in person before committing any money
A: 수리 같은 거는 집주인한테 바로 연락하면 돼요? / B: 네, 집주인분이 근처에 사셔서 바로 오세요.
A: For repairs and such, can I contact the landlord directly? / B: Yes, the landlord lives nearby and comes right over.
수리 ('repairs') — a good 집주인 who lives nearby is a major practical benefit; 한테 is the casual dative particle 'to/for (a person)'
집주인이 좋으셔서 웬만한 건 다 고쳐 주세요.
The landlord's nice, so they fix pretty much everything.
고쳐 주다 ('fixes for you') — this is the outcome of a good 집주인 relationship, worth asking about before you sign
nuance: 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요? is 집주인 ('house owner/landlord') + 이랑 ('with', casual conjunctive particle) + 직접 ('directly/in person') + 얘기하다 ('to talk') + ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can I?'). Asking to speak with the actual owner serves two purposes: (1) building a relationship for repairs and maintenance, and (2) verifying the person signing the contract is truly the registered owner — an important fraud safeguard. The formal real-estate terms are 임대인 (賃貸人, 'lessor/landlord') vs. 임차인 (賃借人, 'lessee/tenant'), used on contracts; in daily speech 집주인 is universal. The dividing line from the agent: the 부동산 (공인중개사, licensed broker) earns a 복비/중개수수료 and brokers the deal, but the 집주인 is the one who makes binding commitments on repairs, rules, and terms — get promises from the owner, not just the agent. The particle 이랑 ('with') is the natural casual choice in speech; 와/과 is formal/written and sounds stiff in conversation. The English-speaker trap is 직역-ing 'directly' as 똑바로 ('straight/upright, physically') — the correct word for 'in person/firsthand' is 직접. Use 존댓말 throughout, including honorifics (집주인분, -세요) when referring to the owner.

structuredNuance.t: 집주인('landlord/owner') + 이랑('with') + 직접('directly/in person') + 얘기하다('talk') + ㄹ 수 있어요?('can I?'). The real purpose is twofold: build a direct relationship for repairs, and verify the person signing is the registered owner — a key fraud-prevention step.

Ask at the contract stage — before money changes hands. 존댓말 always. Refer to the landlord with honorifics even when they're not present: 집주인분, -세요. 반말 (집주인이랑 직접 얘기돼?) only with friends. An agent who refuses to facilitate a meeting with the owner is a red flag.

집주인 (everyday 'landlord') vs. 임대인 (賃貸人, formal 'lessor' on contracts) vs. 집주인분 (honorific form). The agent (부동산/공인중개사) is not the landlord — they earn a 복비 (brokerage fee) and broker the deal; the 집주인 owns the place. Binding promises must come from the 집주인, not the agent.

집주인분은 어떤 분이세요? (what's the landlord like?). 집주인이 같은 건물에 살아요? (do they live on-site?). 수리는 집주인한테 직접 연락하면 돼요? (for repairs, do I contact directly?). 집주인 연락처 받을 수 있어요? (can I get the landlord's contact?).

Two traps: (1) Using 똑바로 instead of 직접 — 똑바로 means 'straight/upright' physically; 직접 means 'in person/firsthand' in dealing with someone. (2) Using 와/과 in speech — 집주인'이랑' 얘기하다 is natural; 집주인'과' 얘기하다 sounds formal/written and stiff in conversation.

mistakes: Saying 똑바로 instead of 직접 for 'directly'.
똑바로 means 'straight/upright' (physically). To deal with someone in person/firsthand, use 직접: 집주인이랑 직접 얘기할 수 있어요?
Using 와/과 in casual speech: 집주인과 얘기할 수 있어요?
와/과 is formal/written. In conversation Koreans say 집주인이랑 or 집주인하고. Save 와/과 for documents.
Assuming the agent is the landlord.
The 부동산 (공인중개사) is a broker who earns a fee (복비); the 집주인 (임대인) owns the place. For binding promises, talk to the owner — and confirm they're the one on the 등기부등본.

english: How much is the agent's fee?
usage: How much is the brokerage fee?
Polite; casual 복비 for the agent's commission
중개수수료 = the formal term, what's on the receipt
Can I get a cash receipt for the fee too?
Asking for a 현금영수증 (cash receipt) for tax/record
examples: 계약하면 복비는 얼마예요?
If I sign, how much is the agent's fee?
Ask this before committing — the 복비 is a real move-in cost that should be in your total budget from the start
A: 중개수수료는 법으로 정해져 있어요? / B: 네, 요율표에 따라서 정해져 있고, 그 이상은 못 받아요.
A: Is the brokerage fee set by law? / B: Yes, it's determined by the rate table, and they can't charge above it.
요율표 ('rate table') is the legal cap — knowing this lets you push back if quoted an inflated fee
복비는 보통 집주인이랑 세입자가 각자 내요.
The fee's usually paid separately by landlord and tenant.
각자 내다 ('each pays their own') — both sides owe the agent; as a tenant you cannot assume the landlord covers it
nuance: 복비는 얼마예요? asks for the real-estate agent's commission. 복비 is a contraction of 복덕방 비(費) — 복덕방 (福德房) being the traditional word for a Korean realtor's office; the modern formal term is 중개수수료 (仲介手數料, 'brokerage fee') or 중개보수. Rates are legally capped on a sliding 요율표 (rate table) based on the property type, deposit, and rent — the fee is not arbitrary, and asking the agent to show the 요율표 is entirely appropriate. Crucially, BOTH the landlord and the tenant each pay their own 복비 to the agent separately (각자 부담) — this surprises newcomers who expect only one side to pay. The dividing line from 보증금/월세 is recipient: 복비 goes to the 부동산 (agent), not the landlord, and it is a ONE-TIME cost at contract, not monthly. The English-speaker trap is treating the Korean agent like a free listing site — the 복비 is a real cost that must be in your move-in budget. Register note: 복비 is the natural spoken word; on receipts and formal documents it is 중개수수료 — recognize both. Also ask 복비도 현금영수증 돼요? ('can I get a cash receipt?') for your records, and verify the agent is a licensed 공인중개사 (certified broker). Stay in 존댓말.

structuredNuance.t: 복비 (colloquial shortening of 복덕방 비(費), 'realtor-office fee') + 는(topic) + 얼마예요?('how much?'). Literally 'how much is the agent fee?' In practice this is an essential total move-in cost question — the fee is legally capped but real, and both landlord and tenant each pay their own.

Ask before committing to a unit so the fee is in your budget. 존댓말 always with the agent. 복비 is natural in speech; 중개수수료 is the formal term on receipts and documents — the agent understands both. 반말 (복비 얼마야?) only with friends.

복비 (casual spoken) = 중개수수료/중개보수 (formal written) — same thing, different register. Dividing line from 보증금/월세: those go to the landlord; 복비 goes to the agent (부동산). 복비 is one-time at contract, not monthly — don't confuse it with 관리비.
중개수수료가 얼마예요? (formal). 요율표 좀 보여 주세요 (show me the rate table). 복비도 현금영수증 돼요? (cash receipt?). 공인중개사 맞으세요? (are you a licensed broker? — a fraud check).

Two traps: (1) Not budgeting for 복비 — unlike in countries where agents are free to the renter, in Korea both sides pay. Budget 월세 + 관리비 + 복비 as your total first-month cost. (2) Register confusion: 복비 is fine in speech, but on a receipt it will say 중개수수료 — recognize both so you know what you signed.

mistakes: Not budgeting for 복비 as a move-in cost.
The agent's commission is a real one-time fee at signing, separate from deposit and rent. Ask 복비는 얼마예요? early so the total cost doesn't surprise you.
Thinking only the landlord pays the agent.
Both sides each pay their own 복비 (각자 부담). As the tenant you owe your own brokerage fee to the 부동산, not just the landlord's.
Treating the fee as freely negotiable like rent.
복비 is capped by a legal 요율표 based on the deposit/rent. It's set within limits, not freely haggled. Ask the agent to show the rate, and request a 현금영수증.
